newsitem.title: BOTSWANA: Botswana weighs parastatal bond issues.
newsitem.headline: Botswana weighs parastatal bond issues.

text.p: Botswana is considering giving the go-ahead for its first ever bond issues by state-owned utilities, a move that could create a secondary bond market in the country, a central bank official said on Thursday.

Bank of Botswana research director Jay Salkin said an inter-departmental task force, including representatives from the Bank, the finance department and individual parastatals, would report on the matter this month.
"I would guess that by the end of next year, we would have had one or more parastatal bonds announced, if not actually in the market," he said in an interview.
The first issuers were likely to be the big three utilities Botswana Telecommunications Corp, Botswana Power Corp and Water Utilities Corp and other borrowers could follow.
Officials are still discussing whether such issues should be targeted at the domestic or international market, Salkin said.
The government of Botswana, bankrolled by revenues from the world's richest diamond fields, has no burning need to raise debt to fund its parastatals.
It runs a budget surplus, has among the world's highest foreign exchange reserves per capita and currently has no state bonds outstanding.
But some economists argue current levels of government support for state concerns are unsustainable in the long term.

The Bank of Botswana has been pushing for some time for the government to tap international capital markets to secure a credit rating from agencies such as Moody's or Standard & Poors, which investors could use to benchmark the country's risk.
Salkin said he was confident Botswana would enjoy a good credit rating, given its political stability and economic health.

That in turn could stimulate investment and help the nascent manufacturing sector, targeted as a key area for expansion under a government diversification plan designed to tackle unemployment afflicting 23-25 percent of the workforce.

"We would argue we should get something like an investment grade rating, given that we have a government that is still running surpluses, we have more than adequate foreign reserves and there are no signs of gross mismanagement or distortions in the economy," he said.

Botswana's foreign exchange reserves stood at 18.4 billion pula at the end of October, equivalent to 29 months import cover, and the government is heading for its 14th consecutive budget surplus this year.
The government has modest outstanding debt of around 1.4 billion pula under loans from foreign governments and international organisations and a debt/service ratio under five percent of GDP.
